# Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/cannabis-and-cannabinoids-in-pd/

# Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.5.1 · generated 2026-11-27 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Positive findings on cannabis in PD come from open-label or uncontrolled designs that the sources treat with caution: a 2026 single-center open-label prospective cohort of 68 patients initiating medical cannabis reported improvements in the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale total score at 3 months, with a dropout rate of 26.5%, and its authors call the findings exploratory; an earlier systematic review states that positive effects described in uncontrolled studies have not been confirmed by the few and small RCTs; and the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement says studies suggesting non-motor benefit are generally small, uncontrolled and open label, and that more rigorous research is needed. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42304702/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32351233/, https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf
- [statement] In the CBD-PD-BRH trial (Parkinsonism & Related Disorders, volume 135, June 2025), sixty PD patients were randomized to sublingual CBD or placebo and 51 were analysed; the authors report that the primary outcome, MoCA delayed recall, showed no group differences, that the CBD group improved naming scores (mean difference 0.37, 95 % CI 0.01 to 0.73) at a mean CBD dose of 26 mg/day, and that alkaline phosphatase was elevated in the CBD group with no serious side effects in either group. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1353802025005826
- [statement] In an exploratory double-blind trial of 21 PD patients without dementia or comorbid psychiatric conditions (placebo, CBD 75 mg/day or CBD 300 mg/day; seven per group), Chagas et al. found no statistically significant differences in UPDRS scores, plasma BDNF levels or H(1)-MRS measures, while mean total PDQ-39 scores differed between the placebo and CBD 300 mg/day groups (p = 0.05); the authors write that their findings point to a possible effect of CBD in improving quality of life measures and that studies with larger samples and specific objectives are required before definitive conclusions can be drawn. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25237116/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] In the Colorado phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral CBD/THC in PD (61 randomized: 31 CBD/THC, 30 placebo; final dose of 2.5mg/kg/day), motor MDS-UPDRS was reduced by 4.57 with CBD/THC and 2.77 with placebo and the between-group difference was not significant (-1.80, p = 0.379); the registry record NCT03582137, which gives the same enrollment window (9/5/2018 to 1/4/2022) and the same 61 randomized, posts a net mean difference of -1.8049 and p = 0.3785; the authors report that sleep, cognition and activities of daily living showed a treatment effect favoring placebo, and conclude that the brief duration and strong placebo response limit interpretation but there was no benefit, perhaps worsened cognition and sleep, and many mild adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11102313/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03582137
- [statement] As published, the Parkinson's Foundation consensus statement (May 2020) says that, given the lack of any clear data supporting the use of cannabis in PD, the Foundation does not endorse its use for PD symptoms or to modify disease progression; the Foundation's web page states that there is no conclusive evidence marijuana helps with PD symptoms; and a document hosted on the Michael J. Fox Foundation website, with content current to March 2022, states that controlled trials have not yet proven the safety or benefit of cannabis in Parkinson's. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/medical-marijuana, https://www.michaeljfox.org/sites/default/files/media/document/Medical_Marijuana_03.04.22.pdf
- [statement] The 2014 American Academy of Neurology systematic review of medical marijuana in selected neurologic disorders concluded that oral cannabis extract is probably ineffective for treating levodopa-induced dyskinesias in patients with Parkinson disease; the PubMed record title of this report carries the label [RETIRED], and the Parkinson's Foundation 2020 statement cites the same AAN conclusion. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24778283/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://www.parkinson.org/sites/default/files/documents/medical_cannabis_statement_finalv2_5.pdf

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported for cannabinoids versus placebo in PD include: the Fernandes et al. meta-analysis of seven randomized trials reports increased risk of confusion (risk ratio, 4.44; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-16.87) and dizziness (risk ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.65-4.68); the Colorado CBD/THC trial reports twice as many treatment emergent adverse events in the CBD/THC group, most of them mild; and the São Paulo cannabis-oil trial reports irritability more frequent in the CBD/THC group (P = 0.005). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11102313/, https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449
- [statement] In Kubota et al. (Movement Disorders, first published 07 August 2026), a phase II randomized, placebo-controlled trial of an oral cannabis oil in PD patients with chronic pain (final daily dosage 43.88 mg CBD and 0.96 mg THC over 9 weeks; 101 randomized, 87 completed), the authors report no significant difference between CBD/THC and placebo in PD-PCS scores (P = 0.757) or in other non-motor scales, and the study was stopped due to futility after a pre-planned interim analysis; the authors conclude that the cannabis oil formulation did not improve pain or other non-motor symptoms compared with placebo. (low confidence) — https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449
- [statement] Randomized trials report different results for non-motor symptoms in PD: Peball et al. (phase II enriched-enrollment randomized withdrawal trial of nabilone; 47 patients began open-label titration and 19 patients received nabilone or placebo) reported a MDS-UPDRS-I difference of 1.63 (95% CI 0.09 to 3.18, p = 0.030) at week 4 and interpret this as potential efficacy of nabilone, with one author an employee of the study-drug manufacturer; Kubota et al. (CBD/THC oil versus placebo) reported no significant differences in other non-motor scales; and the Messak et al. meta-analysis found non-motor symptoms not significantly improved (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32757413/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://movementdisorders.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mds.70449, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis or cannabinoids in PD, published between 2022 and 2026, conclude that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit: Urbi et al. report that no compelling evidence was found to recommend the use of cannabis in PD patients, while also identifying a potential benefit with respect to alleviation of PD related tremor, anxiety, pain, improvement of sleep quality and quality of life; Messak et al. report that cannabinoids have not shown significant benefit in PD; Fernandes et al. report that current randomized evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful benefits. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34958046/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42966680/
- [statement] In the Messak et al. meta-analysis of randomized trials of cannabinoids in PD (eleven RCTs identified, six eligible for meta-analysis), cannabinoids did not significantly improve PD severity (SMD = 0.16, p = 0.27), motor examination (SMD=-0.08, p = 0.57) or non-motor symptoms (SMD= -0.03, p = 0.94); the authors state that the nabilone benefit signal for non-motor symptoms represents a distinct question warranting dedicated trials. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42138778/
- [statement] Two small randomized crossover trials of cannabinoids for levodopa-induced dyskinesia in PD reported opposite results: Sieradzan et al. (Neurology, 2001; n = 7) reported that nabilone significantly reduced levodopa-induced dyskinesia, whereas Carroll et al. (Neurology, 2004; 19 randomized, seventeen completed) reported no evidence of a treatment effect of oral cannabis extract on levodopa-induced dyskinesia; a systematic review of RCTs in movement disorders states that of three PD RCTs with levodopa-induced dyskinesia as primary outcome, only one, using nabilone, showed a reduction. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11739835/ · keywords: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15477546/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35859051/
- [statement] The registry record NCT03582137 (University of Colorado, Denver; cannabidiol for motor symptoms in PD) lists overall status COMPLETED with status verified date 2024-07, lists its phase as PHASE2 with 74 participants enrolled (type ACTUAL), and shows results first posted 2024-07-23. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03582137
- [statement] The registry record NCT06629389 (sponsor Laboratorio Elea Phoenix; a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of cannabidiol (Kanbis) in PD listing its phase as PHASE2, with primary outcome adverse events according to CTCAE v5.0) lists overall status RECRUITING with status verified date 2024-09, estimated primary completion 2025-11 and estimated enrollment 88, and shows no posted results. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06629389
